hook: A seed company prints "85% sprout" on every packet. A garden store plants 200 seeds and only 160 come up: 80%. Is the company exaggerating, or is that just the luck of the draw? To answer, you need to know how much a sample proportion of 200 seeds bounces around when the truth really is 85%.

prereq.q: For a normal distribution with mean 0.85 and standard deviation 0.025, what is the z-score of 0.80?
As the size of a random sample grows, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$
options: stays centered at $p$ and becomes less spread out
moves closer to 0.5 and becomes more spread out
stays centered at $p$ and keeps the same spread
becomes centered at the sample's own proportion
prereq.why: $\hat{p}$ from a random sample is unbiased at every sample size, and larger samples give less variability.

figure.caption: Exact sampling distributions of the proportion of seeds that sprout when p = 0.85. With 200 seeds the normal curve fits; with 20 seeds it does not.

chain.cause: Each sampled seed sprouts (1) or not (0), with a 0-or-1 spread of $\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$
chain.effect: averaging $n$ of them gives $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$, centered at $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$

chain.cause: The sample is drawn without replacement
chain.effect: the formula is accurate only when $n$ is at most 10% of the population: the 10% condition

chain.cause: At least 10 successes and 10 failures are expected ($np \ge 10$, $n(1 - p) \ge 10$)
chain.effect: the sampling distribution is approximately normal: the large counts condition
standardize with $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sigma_{\hat{p}}}$ and find probabilities about $\hat{p}$ from the normal distribution

ideas: $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$ and $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$, using the true $p$.
10% condition: $n$ at most 10% of the population, so the standard deviation formula holds when sampling without replacement.
Large counts condition: $np \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p) \ge 10$, so the shape is approximately normal. Never "$n \ge 30$" for proportions.
When large counts fails, the distribution is skewed: right when $p$ is near 0, left when $p$ is near 1.
Four times the sample size halves $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$.

misconception.wrong: The 10% condition is what makes the distribution of $\hat{p}$ normal, so a sample under 10% of the population can always use a normal model.
misconception.right: The 10% condition protects the standard deviation formula (independence). The normal shape comes from the large counts condition, $np \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p) \ge 10$. Check both, for different reasons.

summary: For random samples, $\hat{p}$ has mean $p$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$ (accurate when the sample is at most 10% of the population) and is approximately normal when $np \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p) \ge 10$. Then $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sigma_{\hat{p}}}$ turns a question about a sample proportion into a normal probability, which you can tie back to a claim about $p$.
